title: The Bird That Says No
concept: Brandon Briggs, a UAA biologist, says the rare earths are not rare; the hard part is concentrating them, which he says can take acids, heat, solvents and 200 steps. His lab already got microbes to do it with coal in the lab but it never scaled to commercial viability. The NSF is funding a $6M project led by Briggs, with UAF, Montana Technological University and Wyoming, to use microbes on coal refuse, with a goal of four or five steps. A deep-learning model led by Masoumeh Heidari Kapourchali will read reactor temperature, acidity, salinity and oxygen, flag a reactor before it fails and a fix, and could quickly flag a bad feedstock instead of months or years, which Briggs says should speed the scale-up. The test: a federally funded pilot elsewhere, by a different method, lost money on paper in every scenario, its own lab recovery ran about 30 percent above its pilot plant for one feedstock, reviews call the field in its infancy, neural networks are usually limited by data, and no results are reported yet. Drawn as NIX, a felt canary holding a card that turns between NO and OK, through seven worlds: a blue-hour lab bench under the Chugach, a map table, a flask cutaway, a top-down reactor bay inside a PLANNED blueprint frame, a corridor planner, a cold street outside another building's pilot, and a dusk wall where Nix aims a reticle card AT the wall beside a dashed GOAL stool, closing from inside a jar.

divergence_note: The last two films were an orbital night kitchen and walnut courtroom with a faced chat-bubble accordion and an auction tag (11-21), and a persimmon-daylight evidence board with a faced suggestion slip (11-19). This film moves through seven worlds (a blue-hour lab bench under the Chugach, a map table, a flask cutaway, a top-down reactor bay in a blueprint frame, a corridor planner, a cold street outside another building's pilot, and a dusk wall exterior in silhouette) with a living hero, a felt canary; its motion is a rise (a wall grows, 200 steps climb, an arrow halts a third of the way, the signature tilt climbs a dashed column), and it closes looking up from inside a jar instead of returning to the window. Honest overlaps: October 9th covered this same NSF project with a faced steel tank, an ember power gauge and a coal ash heap at a dusk frost yard; none of that cast, palette or set returns here, and the thesis is the scale wall, not power. A window onto the Chugach also appeared on 11-21 (kitchen at night), answered by a lab at blue hour.

treatment.title: The Bird That Says No
treatment.summary: The Bird That Says No (Dramatist winner with grafts, restaged at Gate 0B). NIX, a lichen-chartreuse felt canary holding a card that turns between NO and OK, is the deep-learning model, a warning before harm, never a miner. S1 blue-hour lab bench at a window onto the Chugach: a lump of coal refuse thunks into an empty jar beside an empty flask with a blank neck tag; Nix snaps round, its card turning between NO and OK. S2 a faceless Briggs's magnifier hops rock to rock and finds lilac specks in every rock and across the whole range (not rare, per Briggs); specks fly into a motor and a toy turbine; one slips through his fingers, spread thin. S3 a paper staircase unrolls out the window up the Chugach past acid, heat and solvent drums; a faceless hard-hat worker with a hand truck sits down as the counter lands on 200. S4 the microbe crew tips a crumb of refuse into the flask and it blooms lilac (worked before, in the lab), then a cobalt wall rises behind it until it blots out the window. S5 a map table, Canada between Alaska and the lower 48, four pins and a dashed line, a $6M stamp spanning all four, a LED BY BRIGGS tag on Anchorage. S6 a cutaway: microbes squeeze scattered specks into a cluster. S7 a dashed GOAL stool, A HOPE, at the staircase's foot. S8 Nix lands among four dials; a faceless Heidari Kapourchali hangs a frosted DATA feeder, fill hidden, and wires each dial alive. S9 from above, a reactor row inside a PLANNED blueprint frame; Nix raises its card before the foam crests; a microbe spins the valve; FIX. S10 a corridor planner sheds months, a SKIPPED stamp inside a dashed COULD frame sends them flying back, a dashed arrow halts a third of the way up a cobalt stripe (SHOULD, per Briggs). S11 THE TEST: a cold street; Nix and the flickering flask stay on the sidewalk outside another building; its window lights on a dashed ghost pilot tank (DOE-FUNDED PILOT, DIFFERENT METHOD, 2023) and one red-stamped ledger page slaps against the glass. S12 that pilot's own dashed beaker and tank, its LAB bar 3 of 10 blocks taller than its PILOT bar, one feedstock. S13 night bench: a bassinet tagged THE FIELD rocks under a swinging lamp (still in their infancy); a reference feeder for neural networks in general caps at its line while a dashed to-be-gathered line draws on the frosted feeder and a dashed ? on the flask; NO RESULTS YET. S14 dusk silhouette at the wall's foot beside the flask: Nix aims a reticle card AT the wall (not over it), chalk writes AUGUST 2030, the dashed GOAL stool slides out beside the 200 paper steps, and the camera tilts up a dashed plant-scale column to the Chugach. S15 from inside the jar, Nix holds its card edge-on with 2030?, the flask's neck tag turns to AUGUST 2030, and a fresh lump drops in toward camera.
treatment.judge_reasoning: Judge: Dramatist won (cold open 9, arc 8, retention 8, fairness 9, feasibility 8, freshness 8). A coal-mine canary is the thesis in one object, a warning before harm, literally about coal, and it sidesteps the hourglass cliche three pitches reached for. The flask throughline puts the scale wall on screen. Nix never mines and never flies over the wall. Grafts: Explainer's moving microbe cutaway and 200 steps up the Chugach, Comedian's tattletale dials (as four bench dials), Enthusiast's 'aimed at the wall, not over it'. Fixes: Nix flags a reactor not a jar; glacier microbes (c29) cut entirely; can take 200 steps; $6M is the whole project.

angle.thesis: Briggs's lab has already gotten microbes to pull rare earths out of coal in the lab and then hit the scale-up wall, so the AI in this $6M plan isn't a miner, it's a fast no: a model meant to call a failing reactor and a dead-end feedstock early instead of after months or years, which helps Alaska win only if that shortcut survives the jump from lab to plant.
angle.falsifiability: False if, by the award's end in August 2030 (c27), the model's early calls don't shorten the work: reactors it watched fail as often as before (c16, c17), feedstocks it would have ruled out turn out to work, or recovery still drops from lab to larger reactors the way a DOE-funded coal pilot's did (c23). Also false today if the sources gave the AI the extraction job; they don't, the microbes do it (c8, c14).
supporting_facts: The problem is concentration, not scarcity. Per Briggs the rare earths are not rare (c2), the hard part is concentrating them from very dilute sources (c3), and today's route can take strong acids, high temperatures, solvents and 200 steps (c5). He hopes for four or five (c12).

The lab part already worked once and stopped there. His lab has used microbes to pull rare earths from coal before (c32), but the process hasn't been scaled up to be commercially viable (c33). Microbes already recover copper and gold at industrial scale (c13), so biology can scale.

The AI is aimed at time and stability. A deep-learning model led by Masoumeh Heidari Kapourchali (c15) will read temperature, acidity, salinity and oxygen (c14), say when a reactor's going to fail and what corrections could prevent it (c16, c17), and could quickly say a feedstock won't work instead of months if not years of trials (c34); NSF adds a virtual assay to screen feedstocks (c18). Briggs says it should speed the scale-up (c25).
angle.counterpoint_to_honor: THE TEST, at full strength. Scale is where this field breaks. A DOE-funded pilot that pulled rare earths from coal material lost money on paper in every scenario (c22, a different, chemical-leach route, not UAA's), and for one feedstock its lab recovery ran about 30 percent higher than the pilot plant (c23). Reviews call bioleaching rare earths from waste still in its infancy (c24). And a neural network is usually limited by how much data it has (c26), while a new process starts with little, so the model may be weakest where it's needed most. Nothing is reported yet (c28). The film survives this by narrowing honestly: it claims the AI is aimed at the right wall, not that it gets over it.
angle.who_it_serves: Alaskans weighing whether coal waste can be a critical-minerals asset (legislators, UA, economic development staff) who get a concrete test for 2030 (did the early no save trials, did recovery hold at scale); UAA and UAF researchers; anyone reading AI in a grant headline who wants to know what the model actually does.
angle.second_movement: The reveal that recontextualises the hopeful open: UAA's own lab already did the hard-sounding part in the lab (c32) and stalled at scale (c33). So the grant is not a bet on new biology, it's a bet on a tool that says no faster. Then the test scene (c22, c23, c24, c26) and the turn: the four-or-five-step goal (c12) and the August 2030 end (c27) are the scoreboard.

runner_up_angles.thesis: A: the AI is aimed at the exact wall that stops microbial rare-earth recovery leaving the lab, the right bet not a buzzword
runner_up_angles.why_lost: the right bet is a verdict on work with no results (c28); the room downgraded it to the right target, which the winner keeps

runner_up_angles.thesis: B: the AI is UAA's bet on the stage where a federally funded attempt lost money
runner_up_angles.why_lost: borrowed a different, chemical route's losses as if the same process failed; kept as the Act 3 test, not the thesis

runner_up_angles.thesis: C: a shorter miner, the predictor must make a four-or-five-step living process dependable
runner_up_angles.why_lost: treated the goal as the mechanism's job and wrote as many as 200, against c5; its time framing was grafted in

runner_up_angles.thesis: October 9th's thesis, the second AI is built around variable power
runner_up_angles.why_lost: already shipped 44 days ago; energy appears at most as a clause

angle.absence_checks: NSF 2614749 abstractText and every ML paragraph of the UAA release searched for training data, data volume, reactor count and an Alaska coal feedstock: none stated (say not stated, never none exist). OSTI 1971736 abstract searched: no machine learning; describes bio-oxidation reactors making bio-acid, so never say no microbes were involved there.

hook.headline: AN AI BUILT TO SAY NO · FAST
hook.loopback: Frame 1 is a lump thunking into the empty jar as Nix snaps round with a card turning between NO and OK; the last shot looks up from inside that jar at Nix holding the card with a question mark, as a fresh lump drops in beside it.

open_loop.what: Will this ever work at full size? Planted with the empty flask's BLANK neck tag beside the jar as the lump lands, carried as the flask glows, meets the wall, dims on the street outside another building's pilot and takes a dashed ? on its fill line, paid when chalk writes AUGUST 2030 on the wall above Nix, the date the award ends.

open_loop_2.what: How much will it learn from? Planted when Heidari Kapourchali hangs a FROSTED feeder tagged DATA whose fill is hidden, paid when a small reference feeder labelled NEURAL NETWORKS GENERALLY swings beside it and a dashed TO BE GATHERED line draws on the frosted glass: how much the model learns depends on what goes in, and the amount isn't stated.
